Some of the statistics are pretty even but Atletico Madrid have had just three touches in the Liverpool penalty area, yet have a goal to their name.

The first half at Anfield is brought to an end and it is level at 1-1 at the break. Llorente gave Atletico the lead before Szoboszlai equalised for Liverpool. The home fans let the officials know what they think of their performance in that first half.

One added minute at the end of this first half.

There has been about five minutes of squabbling between the Liverpool and Atletico benches, so much so that Tommy Elphick - Andoni Iraola’s assistant - missed Dominik Szoboszlai score the equaliser. Tensions have only increased after a nasty little challenge from Cristian Romero on Alexander Isak. The half-time whistle might be coming at a good time to defuse the situation but you fancy the walk back to the dressing rooms will be spicy.

The conduct of the Atletico players is frankly embarrassing, not a massive surprise from a Diego Simeone side. Kang goes down clutching his face when there was barely any contact and then, unlike Isak, he does not have to spend a minute off the pitch.

Isak is on the ground, clutching at his knee, after a heavy challenge from Romero. It is a nasty challenge from Romero, who remarkably is neither booked nor penalised. To compound the awful officiating, Isak now has to spend a minute off the pitch owing to the new rules. What do you make of that new rule of the player who is down going off for a minute? Have your say in the comments section at the bottom of the blog.

Moments after Liverpool equalised, Atletico have a decent opportunity to restore their lead but Baena drags his effort wide from the edge of the box.

Moments after Barcola could not take a big chance to equalise for Liverpool, Szoboslzai does. First, Barcola is denied by Oblak. Liverpool keep it alive inside the Atletico box and a simple sensational flick by Aruajo finds Szoboszlai, who finds the bottom corner with a clinical finish. Kerkez has been poor tonight but he deserves credit for his part in that goal as he was the player to initially win it back for Liverpool with a good press.

Szoboszlai slots home after a brilliant flick from Araujo! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UrHQTwtgsY

Liverpool look like a team that has been out of the Champions League for a couple of years and are only just finding its feet, which seems strange given they missed only one year in the last 10. They have glimmers of promise but they aren’t convincing anyone they will blow Atleti’s house down. One day everything will align for Atleti and they will reach another final. They have an outside chance this year, especially if Julian Alvarez - easily the best player on this pitch - has anything to do with it. Diego Simeone always has class strikers at the top of his team and Alvarez stands comparison with any who have gone before.

Wirtz has a great chance to equalise for Liverpool but his shot on the half volley is saved by Oblak. It would not have mattered anyway had the ball ended up in the net because Isak was offside before crossing for Wirtz.

Some of the officiating tonight has been appalling and the latest example is VAR taking a check on a possible red card for Mac Allister for a foul that is never a red card in a million years. The officials then take an age to give yet another obvious offside and, in the end, the referee gives it rather than the linesman. That really does sum up the officials tonight as the referee should not be the one to give offsides.

Alvarez shoots from distance and forces Alisson into a good save diving to his right. There was a suspicion of offside from Simeone in the build-up.

Atletico take it short but Simeone’s shot is blocked by Araujo.

The Anfield faithful are furious. Two fouls in quick succession are not given when they were both clearly fouls. The referee appears to have a different interpretation of body checks and taking people out off the ball than the rest of us.

The Spanish side take the lead at Anfield and it is another goal on this ground for Llorente. Alvarez feeds a through ball to pick out the run of Llorente, who is onside. He takes one touch before firing past Alisson from the edge of the box. That is poor, poor defending from Kerkez, who not only played Llorente onside but then did not track the run properly. Llorente now has five goals on this ground.

Llorente breaks the deadlock! 🔥That's now FIVE Champions League goals for the Atletico man against Liverpool at Anfield 🤯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Rxp4zurfpc

The idea that Atletico Madrid are focused on spoiling and nullifying belongs in the past. They are an attractive team, well organised and you suspect they have the gears to cause Liverpool problems... and as we type, they have just opened the scoring by playing straight through Liverpool’s middle. It was a bad goal for home side to concede. Milos Kerkez was out of sync with the rest of Liverpool’s defence and Marcos Llorente has galloped straight through. As we said at the start: it’s a big test for the hosts... it’s just got even bigger.

A little line about Llorente, who has now scored five times against Liverpool in the Champions League. He is fond of playing in this arena, he named his dog “Anfield! when he bought it in 2021.

Chance for Barcola. Szoboszlai clips a lovely ball in behind down the right channel to pick out the run of Barcola. The Frenchman takes it down beautifully before having his shot saved by Oblak. Barcola’s best moment thus far tonight.

Baena takes a first-time effort on from a central position around 25 yards out but he cannot keep his effort down and it sails into The Kop.

Atletico were renowned for years under Diego Simeone is being very tight at the back and in midfield, especially away from home. However, in recent years they have become more expansive and as a result are more open.

Liverpool win their first corner of the night at the Anfield Road End in front of the travelling Atletico fans. They take it short and Szoboslzai takes it towards the Atletico box. It appeared to be a very obvious foul on Szoboszlai right on the edge of the box but nothing is given. At the very least, it should have been given a free-kick as there was definitely at least one foul.

Barcola, who has won the Champions League with PSG in the last two seasons, is starting out on the right for Liverpool tonight with Ngumoha on the left.

Big test for Liverpool and it will be fascinating to see how this formation works out. It looks very much like it is 4-4-2, with Florian Wirtz almost alongside Alexander Isak and Rio Ngumoha the left winger and Bradley Barcola on the opposite flank - a position Andoni Iraola has referenced him playing in Lyon as a teenager. It’s also a big test for Iraola against Diego Simeone, the wily and vastly experienced manager, who is immaculately dressed - as always - in his trademark black suit.

Liverpool have a chance inside the opening minute. Szoboszlai wins it inside his own half and drives forward. He then plays it out to his right to find Isak, whose shot from the right side of the box is dragged wide of the far post. Isak did score from a similar position against Ipswich last Friday, when he scored at the near post.

A minute’s silence to remember the victims of the landslides in Nepal is impeccably observed.

We are under way at Anfield. Liverpool’s Champions League campaign gets going as Andoni Iraola takes charge of his first game as a manager in this competition.

The two sides emerge from the tunnel to a cacophony of noise and we are moments away from kick-off at Anfield. The home fans boo the Champions League anthem and belt out “Liverpool! Liverpool!” over the top of it. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

The original “This is Anfield” sign has sold at auction for almost £150,000, 10 times more than its guide price.

The sign that hung above the players’ tunnel at Liverpool’s home stadium during the 1970s had been expected to fetch between £10,000 and £15,000 after being put up for auction on Tuesday and Wednesday.

But the “talismanic” piece of football memorabilia ended up being sold by auctioneer Budds for £149,500 to a UK private buyer.

The Argentine is into the final two years of his contract, which runs out in 2028. He arrived at Liverpool in the same summer as fellow midfielders Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai, who have both signed new contracts. Mac Allister was linked with a move away from Liverpool during the summer transfer window and was candid about his contractual situation in the press conference yesterday:

“I received the news that the club was not in a position to offer me a new contract which, of course, makes me very, very sad. Everyone can see that I give my 100% for this football club every single day in training and games. Of course, I can have very good games [and] bad games, like everyone, but I always give my best.

“I see Dominik [Szoboszlai] and Ryan [Gravenberch] renewing their contracts and that makes me very happy because they deserve it. At the same time it makes me a little bit sad that I did not get mine. Of course, there is still time. The fans do not need to worry because I will give my 100% until the last day I am here. There were options to leave this summer. I think right now I am in the right club and I have the right mindset to give 100% for this club.”

Former Liverpool manager Rafa Benitez, who led the club to Champions League glory on that famous night in Istanbul in 2005, is in attendance tonight. Andoni Iraola has just shared a hug with his compatriot and perhaps Benitez will have a few words of advice for Iraola ahead of his Champions League debut as a manager.

The Dutchman has been in fine form at the start of the season for Liverpool, registering a goal and three assists in his first three games. He missed training yesterday and is not in Liverpool’s matchday squad tonight. Andoni Iraola has confirmed that Gakpo has a small adductor injury that he picked up in the Ipswich game last Friday but could be fit for the weekend against Fulham.

Liverpool: Alisson; Araujo, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Kerkez; Mac Allister, Szoboszlai; Ngumoha, Wirtz, Barcola; Isak.Substitutes: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Tsimikas, Munoz, Frimpong, Gravenberch, Nyoni, Chambers, McConnell, Koumas, Danns.

When Liverpool won their sixth European Cup in 2019, they lifted it in the Wanda Metropolitano against Tottenham. This season’s Champions League final is in that very stadium and Liverpool’s Champions League campaign starts tonight against the club that plays their home games in that stadium, Atletico Madrid.

“This is going to be a challenge, I hope, all the season because it would mean we continue in all the competitions. In this case, it is not the worst scenario because we played last Friday so we have had I think a good recovery. Probably it is going to be more difficult for next weekend, especially for the next game against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup because we will have just two days, game, two days, game. But we have to get used to this; it is what big clubs do. Definitely there is part of your mind where you have to think [about] the next games. But for us, the game tomorrow is very important.”

Ready for #UCL action 👊🔴 pic.twitter.com/XyOupLwsRe

Liverpool begin their Champions League campaign at home as they host Atletico Madrid at Anfield. These sides met at Anfield on matchday one last season, with Liverpool winning a dramatic game 3-2. Liverpool led 2-0 inside the opening 10 minutes before Atletico came back to level the game at 2-2. Virgil van Dijk then scored in added time to give Liverpool all three points before Atletico boss Diego Simeone was sent off for clashing with the Anfield crowd, resulting in a one-match ban.

Andoni Iraola earned his first win as Liverpool boss on Friday night as they won 2-0 away at Ipswich thanks to a quickfire early double from Alexander Isak. This will be Iraola’s first Champions League match as a manager.

“I think obviously it is a special night for me,” Iraola said. “Everyone talks [about] the Champions League nights at Anfield and also the first game is against a strong opposition, it is Atletico Madrid. [Diego] Simeone is doing an incredible job as a manager. To be all the years that he has been achieving every season the goals of the club I think is remarkable and definitely it is a big challenge for us. I think I played against him as a player, he was still a player, and I played against his teams when he was a coach and I also coached against him. So, we had a lot of precedent before. Definitely he has much more experience than me in this kind of games but I hope tomorrow we can give him a good game.

“It is one of the dreams, probably, when you start. It was difficult for me when I started my coaching career seven, eight years ago, to position myself in the position that I am right now, and I hope I can enjoy it. It is a big responsibility, massive challenge, but I feel privileged to be there in that dugout tomorrow [tonight] and now my thinking is about putting the team together in a position where we can play a good game, win the game and start strong in this Champions League.”

Atletico Madrid currently sit sixth in La Liga and suffered their first defeat on Saturday as they lost 3-0 at Athletic Bilbao. They did reach the semi-finals of the Champions League last season, where they fell to Arsenal 2-1 on aggregate.

“We are coming into a marvellous stadium and there will be a great atmosphere,” Simeone said. “We will have to look good from the start of the game because it will be full on. He [Andoni Iraola] works very well with the team, focusing on the tactical awareness of each player. It takes time to find the right path, but he is growing and improving and he has some very good players.”

Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1936. Scotland are failing to dispel emperor’s new clothes concerns after laboured victory

The Scottish Football Association’s ticket promotion drive for this match emphasised that games are always better under the lights. They might need to re-think that one.

This was another endurance test that at least had a satisfactory outcome, courtesy of John McGinn’s double. In between times a goal for North Macedonia - their first in nine games - probably triggered a national holiday back home and made things look very difficult indeed for Sebastien Pocognoli.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Scotland held onto their lead, given to them after McGinn drove into the box following strong centre-forward play from Che Adams, for the best part of three minutes.

A penalty, awarded after a VAR check a good couple of minutes after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski's trip on Ben Gannon-Doak occurred, saved Scotland’s blushes with 16 minutes left and kept their Nations League hopes just about alive.

McGinn did the necessary from the spot although Oli McBurnie, who had replaced Adams six minutes earlier, might have appreciated being given the ball in his seemingly eternal quest for an international goal. It was perhaps too important a kick to take any chances. A manager’s future prospects might have rested on it.

It was a case of third time lucky for Pocognoli as he secured his first Hampden win on what had not seemed like a particularly auspicious date. For the first time since the notorious 0-0 draw against Uruguay that torpedoed their 1986 World Cup, Scotland were in action on a Friday the 13th. What could possibly go wrong? A lot, it seemed at times.

If anything underlined that these are very different times for Scotland it was the sight of Scott McTominay, almost a year to the day since that overhead kick against Denmark, launching himself into the air again in an effort to meet Gilmour’s cross. Although he connected well, the direction was lacking. The ball went high over the bar.

There was no goal from the halfway line this time either. Instead, we were treated to one of the worst misses ever seen at Hampden when Gilmour skied the ball from seven yards seconds after the interval.

The Hampden crowd was getting testy. Boos had greeted the half-time whistle, with the score still goalless and the hosts perhaps lucky not to have conceded.

McGinn’s opener ten minutes after half-time seemed like just the medicine. However, underlining how this was never straightforward, Macedonia equalised almost immediately. They had to score a goal sometime but it was not a good look for Scotland or McTominay, who was beaten in the air at the front post by Elmin Rastodar following a corner.

A clumsy challenge at the other end by Dimitrievski on Gannon-Doak, whose poor touch had already looked to have taken the chance away from him, gave Scotland the gratifying chance to equalise from the spot 17 minutes later.

The hosts had endured an uncertain start that was a decent indicator of what lay ahead. What seemed like teething problems might have been attributed to a defence playing together for the first time. Ryan Porteous was brought back into the starting line-up, his first start since the opening match of Euro 2024 when he was sent off.

Luke Graham, meanwhile, earned his second cap - a first start for Scotland - and was planted right in the middle of the three-man backline. After surviving a few shaky moments initially, the Stoke City defender acquitted himself superbly well.

North Macedonia’s dismal run, which included not having scored in this Nations League campaign so far, perhaps convinced Pocognoli he could make such alterations though injury had restricted his options. Poertoeus, though, hadn’t even been named in the original squad.

Defence wasn’t expected to be an issue. It was a Friday night after a long week at work. Fans wanted to be entertained, they wanted to see some tangible evidence of a new Scotland they have been promised. Pocognoli might wear a suit very well but he’s not proved himself to be his predecessor’s equal at obtaining results, although this was more like it. The fear is that this supposedly more free-flowing Scotland has made them blunter. The phrase the emperor’s new clothes could not be banished from the mind.

Not even McTominay could ignite things. He seemed ready to burst the net just a few minutes later after Lewis Ferguson’s header found the Napoli midfielder with his back to goal in the box. When he turned, it looked like there would be only one outcome. However, Dimitrievski made a tremendous save low to his left.

Yes, this was another occasion where the North Macedonian goalkeeper excelled himself, just as he did in Skopje at the start of last month.

Another save, when he plucked a deflected Adams header out from beneath his crossbar, was even better. There were mitigating factors for Scotland failing to make the breakthrough in the opening half.

It might have been worse for the home team. A cute lay-off from Darko Churlinov set up skipper Enis Bardhi, who lashed a left-footed shot into the side-netting. Most of the Hampden crowd feared the ball had gone in. The smattering of North Macedonia fans were beside themselves.

Sadly for them, happily for the vast majority, the rippling effect was due to the ball hitting the wrong side of the net. It might have been marginally offside in any case. Jeers greeted the blowing of the half-time whistle moments later, nonetheless.

Would Scotland come out with a renewed sense of purpose? It seemed so. Adams pounced on a short pass back and cut the ball back while Dimitrievski dithered.

Billy Gilmour is no one’s idea of a prolific goalscorer but even he couldn’t miss from seven yards, goal gaping. He did. Quite incredibly, the ball comfortably cleared the bar. People were referencing Chris Iwelumo, meaning it was one of the worst misses of all time. It was at the right end, certainly. McGinn showed him how to do it, moving level with Hughie Gallacher in third place on 24 goals in the all-time list of goalscorers and ensuring Andy Robertson’s record-equalling 102nd cap would also be the victorious one the skipper deserved.

#1935. Simon Leslie: We wanted an Eastbourne Borough response – and got it in style under the lights

On another afternoon it could have finished 6-1 to Borough, but they scored four from five shots on target and we managed one from ten. Sometimes football leaves you wondering how on earth you have lost a game like that.

Our fans, however, were amazing. You sang and sang, even when there was no way back. When you have travelled to support your team and the afternoon goes against you, that takes some doing. Thank you.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

I did wonder whether the manager of the month curse had struck again! Congratulations to Steve King on his thoroughly deserved award. One difficult afternoon certainly doesn’t undo the work that earned it.

What mattered next was how the boys responded, and Tuesday evening against Dulwich Hamlet gave us plenty to be proud of.

Conceding in the second minute was hardly the start we wanted. After Saturday, it would have been easy for heads to drop. Instead, these boys worked their socks off and went into half-time 3-1 up.

The second half was harder going in the rain, but the boys stuck at it and came away with a 4-2 win. A proper response to Saturday and three very welcome points, especially as Welling dropped a couple of points down the road.

Bobby, our commentator, and I both had Liam Nash as our man of the match. Considering he has been out for so many weeks, he was amazing. It was lovely to see him back playing so well.

It was bitterly cold, too. To everyone who came out, wrapped up and got behind the team, thank you. There are certainly warmer ways to spend a Tuesday evening, and we appreciate you choosing to spend yours with us.

Tomorrow is a huge occasion as Chertsey Town visit for an FA Trophy second round tie. I would love to see a big crowd at Priory Lane helping the boys take another step in the competition. Bring a friend, bring the family and bring your voices. A few extra layers might be sensible as well!

We have also had another trophy to celebrate. Our Spirit of Football team recently paraded their first silverware in front of a packed stadium, and we are so proud of every one of them. Seeing the reception they received was a lovely moment for everyone involved.

As the weather gets more miserable, there is plenty happening indoors at the club. Padel is great fun for all ages, good exercise and, judging by everyone who has tried it, highly addictive. Come down and give it a go.

Our new simulators also let you play golf at thousands of courses, with all the excitement and no wet clothes afterwards. Both the Padel Centre and Simulator Centre make great Christmas party venues, whether you are getting together with friends, family or work colleagues.

For now, though, let’s get behind the boys tomorrow and make it another cup afternoon to remember.

Resd EBFC owner Simon Leslie’s column in the Herald and on this website throughout the season

#1934. Sebastien Pocognoli predicts another Scotland record will be broken and identifies ‘something we need to fix’

Sebastien Pocognoli believes it is only a matter of time until John McGinn becomes Scotland’s all-time top goalscorer.

The Scotland manager saw McGinn score a match-winning double to help Scotland secure a scratchy and often uninspired win over North Macedonia. It handed Pocognoli his first Hampden victory at the third attempt and brought some relief for the Belgian.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It hadn’t looked good when North Macedonia equalised almost immediately after McGinn had put Scotland ahead after 54 minutes. The header from Elmin Rastoder was the visitors' first goal in nine games.

A penalty from McGinn following a VAR check with 16 minutes left, after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski clumsily tripped Ben Gannon-Doak, secured the three points for Scotland and kept their hopes of finishing second in their Nations League group alive. Slovenia drew 0-0 with group winners Switzerland.

Pocognoli’s side must win against Switzerland in St Gallen on Monday and hope Macedonia take something from their clash at home against the Slovenians.

With McGinn in the side, anything is possible against Switzerland. Pocognoli hailed the Aston Villa’s contribution and feels he will shortly overtake Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law in the rankings. Both legends scored 30 goals for Scotland and McGinn, who now sits third with Hughie Gallacher on 24 goals, is now just seven goals from overtaking the pair at the top. He has already scored three goals under Pocognoli, having struck a penalty in the 2-0 win against North Macedonia in Skopje last month.

“I'm more focused on the collective challenge and goals,” said Pocognoli. “And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record. He has had a lot of chances through these five games together already. It's important but the individual record I always bring in the collective package. And I hope for him that he can reach it.”

Pocognoli, if not satisfied with all aspects of Scotland’s play, was happy to end the week “with a good feeling” and before travelling to face Switzerland.

He added: “It was not always perfect, but I know that what we worked in two days (this week) happened many times today on the pitch. That's for me very important. On top of that, we created a lot of chances that we really have to score and maybe have a better feeling after the game. But on the whole, I think we were quite aggressive.”

Billy Gilmour missed an open goal shortly after half-time while Dimitrievski pulled off a number of good saves.

“Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive,” said Pocognoli, who handed a full debut to Stoke City’s Luke Graham in the centre of a three-man defence. “We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

"We created a big chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that's a new approach of the game. I think we started the game not that intensely because we didn't manage the ball well. And then for sure you start the game with the feeling that we don't control the ball. After 10 minutes we started to reach Lewis [Ferguson] and Billy [Gilmour] through the lines. And then the game became what we expected.

‘We created chances, we isolated Ben [Gannon-Doak] in the one v one, and we had a lot of pressure. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for 5 minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus.

“And we had the same feeling after the second one. So, it's something that we need to fix.”

He agreed Scotland need to be more clinical. “Yes, probably,” he said, while perhaps recalling the missed chances against Slovenia in his first match in charge and which now seem so significant.

‘But I prefer to talk about creating a lot of chances,” he added. “And probably we should keep a clean sheet. So that's really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect. But it's part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.”

#1931. ‘Ahead of where we thought we’d be’ – Dolan says home defeats won’t derail Hastings United

United went down 3-0 to Sevenoaks on Tuesday night, soon after home reverses to Faversham and Deal. It was a setback after a fine 3-0 win at Cray Valley PM had put them back on top of the Isthmian South East table.

Dolan insists it’s still been a great start to the season and they’re ahead of where they expected to be. And he’s ready to try to get them back to their best home form against Steyning tomorrow.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

"Sevenoaks are another very good team – they move the ball well and work hard as a team – they’re very athletic and quick on the counter.

"We weren’t really at the races. As much as we were battling we weren’t really hurting them like we should have done or how we know we can. That’s something we’re looking to rectify.

"The red card didn’t have a big effect on the game, I don’t think. We’ll never know if having 11 men would have kept us in the game til the end and got us a point or something out of the game. We can’t do much about that.

"There wasn’t much in it to be a red card but it’s two yellows and that’s the way it is in football these days – you have to be very careful.

"But our performance wasn’t ‘at it’ – and that’s maybe down to a lot of games in short space of time. I think in the past couple of months we’ve only had one week where we haven’t had a Tuesday game. We’ve played a lot of games in a short space of time, as has everyone, but I think we’re running on a slightly smaller squad, though a very good squad.

"That’s always going to take its toll at some point. It’s now a case of can we freshen it, can we build on it, can we look to add one or two to freshen the squad up a little and see what we can do from there. We’ve got another Saturday-Tuesday this week and there’s a lot of football to play in the season.

"We’ve come through this period doing okay – we’re okay in the league, we have a lot of points on the board considering we’re a very yojng squad and we’ve rebuilt in the summer. I think we’re ahead of where we expected to be so all in all I’m pretty happy – it’s just a case of can we add to it and try to find more consistency as a team.”

Asked if home form dip could be down to nerves he said he didn’t. “I think it’s a blip that we’ll get over. We started off so well at home this season and it’s now a case of can we freshen it up a little, whether that’s bringing players in or rotating players we have in the squad already and trying to find the right formula at home again – whether that’s changing shape or changing personnel.

"We’ll look into those things as a management but I do think everyone during a season knows you’re not going to win every home. It’s not ideal losing three home games in a row so we’ll look at it. Whoever can keep that consistency through the season will do well. Having a young and newly built squad, it’s hard to get that consistency.

"It’ll take a bit of time but we’re ahead of where we wanted to be this season. I’m pretty pleased and we’ll see how we go from here.”

Three days earlier it was a 3-0 win at Cray Valley PM courtesy of goals by Kes Clarke, Warren Mfula and Sam Pidgeon.

Dolan said: “Iit was a good win. I wouldn’t say we were on top from the word go. They created quite a few opportunities first half which ex expcted, because they’re a good team with very good players in attacking areas.

"We expected them to come at us and, being at home, to creat opportunities, which they did. But unfortunately for them, they didn’t take them – and when we created our own chances, we did and we punished them.

"I keep saying to our boys, when we get opportunities we have to punish teams.Normally we get punished so it was nice for us to be on the other side of it, punishing a team for not taking their chances.

"The second half we dominated – I think they only had one shot in the half and it was a fairly comfortable save for Harry. So it was a good away win and good performance all round.

It’s Steyning next at the Pilot Field and Dolan said: “Every game is tricky – every opposition team have their own threats and can cause you problems. We have to concentrate on how we deal with that and get on the front foot, and can we create and take chances. I genuinely think that if we go back to what we were doing at the start of the season, particularly at home, teams won’t be able to deal with us. We’ve got to find that consistency.

"Steyning we will give the respect they deserve. We’ll have trained hard and gone over a few things but we expect a tough game. Every game in this league. We aim to go into Saturday and look to rectify Tuesday.

"Then we have Whitehawk in the senior cup. You want to win every game, whether it’s a cup or league match. And with the final being at the Amex, it would be amazing to get there. If we win it’s happy days but if we fall short yet we’ve turned up and put in a performance but luck isn’t on our side, that’s fair enough. But we want to win it."

#1928. GdS: Fluidity, gifts and a tense finale – how Milan overcame Genoa to reclaim top four spot

AC Milan won away from home against an in-form Genoa side to ensure they will go into the international break inside the top four.

La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) have analysed a second consecutive Serie A victory for Milan, remarking that if it were it not for the nuisance of the Europa League – specifically that ugly defeat to Ferencváros – they would be heading into the break in perfect spirits.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Still, things have worked out well enough: the win at Marassi, combined with Como’s loss against Inter, has allowed Rúben Amorim’s side to leapfrog Cesc Fàbregas’s team and move into fourth place. It is of course the final spot for Champions League qualification, the minimum objective.

The question remains the same: which is the ‘real’ Milan? The one that put two goals past Genoa in the opening 20 minutes, or the one that nearly threw it all away with a passive final 20 minutes of the game?

Daniele De Rossi almost snatched a point thanks to his substitutions, while Amorim nearly dropped two points due to his own, less-than-effective changes. It seems clear that there is an issue with the squad’s overall competitiveness, with help needed in January.

In Genoa, Amorim opted for a 4-4-2 formation to start, with Yunus Musah deployed as a surprise left-back and a central midfield pairing of Luka Modrić and Adrien Rabiot.

Just seconds after kick-off, Genoa nearly took a 1-0 lead through Osmajic, who surged deep into the final third. Shaken into life by this, Milan took control and built a 2-0 lead.

In the second half, the team gradually shifted into a classic 3-5-2, eventually dropping into a five-man defensive line to hold firm after Ellertsson’s goal. In modern football, fluidity is an asset though it carries the risk of lacking a clear, defined identity.

Milan dominated for long stretches of the first half, particularly on the flanks, but found themselves under significant duress toward the end of the match. The data on the average position of the team is telling: Genoa finished at 55.6 metres, while Milan sat at 44.3.

Anyone unaware of the final score when looking at the stats might well imagine a different outcome, while it remains unclear if the team dropping so deep was instruction or protective instinct. However, the Diavolo survived.

The reality is that sometimes errors – individual or otherwise – have a greater impact on results than good intentions or tactical formations. Genoa arrived at this match on the back of three consecutive victories, though they were missing Frendrup, the Dane who acts as the team’s stabiliser.

Having already enjoyed a string of successes, the team grew complacent. It was a feeling only intensified by the golden opportunity that fell to Osmajic in the opening minutes. Genoa lulled themselves into a false sense of security, and some players began to switch off.

There was an early warning sign when Vasquez gifted the ball to Gonçalo Ramos, though the Portuguese forward’s shot went wide. Later, Vasquez was dispossessed again – this time by Pulisic – sparking the sequence that led to the 0-1 goal: a touch to Rabiot, a cross for Cissé and a finish.

Milan then shifted their focus to the left flank. Under pressure from Cissé, Traoré played a disastrous pass toward Østigård inside the box. The Norwegian failed to clear it, and Ramos set up Pulisic just inside the area for the goal that made it 0-2.

At 2-0, the game opened up for Milan, who favoured direct, vertical play over patient possession. The attacking combinations on the flanks proved decisive: Moreira operated on one side, working alongside Pulisic, who was given the freedom to roam between the penalty area, the final third, and the wing.

The duo of Musah and Cissé dominated their flank against Marcandalli and Ehizibue. Deploying Musah as a left-back was a tactical move De Rossi likely hadn’t anticipated. Was it all over? Had the match been decided? Not quite. Before the half-time whistle, Genoa showed signs of a resurgence.

In the second half, the atmosphere turned hostile, and referee Massa had to send four people off from the benches to restore some semblance of order. Then, a flurry of substitutions narrowed the gap between Genoa and Milan.

When El Shaarawy came on, De Rossi found more space to push forward. When Pulisic was taken off, Amorim’s side lost ground. Ellertsson’s goal – a beautiful strike, aided by a lack of marking from Jashari – set the stall out for a frantic final stretch, during which Milan risked conceding an equaliser.

if you tally up the chances and shots on target, the scales actually tip in favor of the Grifone. So, what does this mean? Is all well that ends well? Is a Champions League spot guaranteed? Certainly not. The impression is that this Milan is still in a phase where anything is possible, in either direction.

A return to the Champions League is far from certain, but the table is tight. League-leaders Lazio are only five points ahead, less than two wins away, so who’s to say Milan can’t aim higher?

Much will depend on January. The winter window shouldn’t be about patching things up, as quick fixes often end up being worse than the original problems. Rather, Gerry Cardinale (plus potentially Markus Krösche) should think about genuine improvement.

It will also depend on Amorim and his ability to shape the squad, ironing out the deficiencies. In the background, the question of Gonçalo Ramos remains. He showed commendable selflessness at Marassi, but he needs to start scoring himself soon.

For now, Cissé is stepping up, having netted his eighth goal of the season and his fifth in Serie A. Roberto Mancini is now waiting for him with the senior national team, which is just the latest step in a fairytale start to 2026-27.

#1927. ‘Angry with myself’ - Brighton star Jack Hinshelwood opens up on injury blow

Brighton midfielder Jack Hinshelwood had a topsy turvy start to the new season.

Hinshelwood, 21, scored twice in the 4-0 win against Aston Villa on the opening day of the 2026-27 campaign but then swiftly sustained an injury to his quad during the next training session.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The England under-21 international missed the Premier League matches against Chelsea, Leeds, Coventry, Arsenal and Sunderland.

He returned and featured in Conference League fixtures against Kauno Zalgiris, Jablonec and Getafe and also made substitute appearances in the Premier League against Crystal Palace (he scored), Liverpool, Manchester City and Brentford.

Hinshelwood is starting to get back to his top form but faces a battle to regain his starting position as the likes of Yasin Ayari, Malick Yalcouye, Pascal Gross and Chema Andres have performed so well in his absence.

“I was a bit unlucky after the Villa game,” Hinshelwood said to the Albion website.

“In training, I just struck a ball and felt my quad a little bit, so I had some time out after that. I was very frustrated because you come off the back of scoring two goals and then you’re not fit for six weeks.

“The first few weeks were tough, and I was probably a bit angry with myself just because of the way it happened. But then you get over it and you’re just working hard to get back amongst it.”

Brighton have enjoyed a fine start to the season and last Sunday’s 2-0 win against Brentford moved them second in the table.

Brighton - along with the rest of the Premier League - are currently paused for the international break and resume action on November 22 at Hull City.

Hinshelwood added: “The boys were in great form and still are, so that made it a little bit easier during the tough time. Now I’m just trying to come back, support the team, and get back in the starting line-up.

“They’re doing so well, so I’m pushing for every opportunity I get to try and do my best to help the team move forward.”

Hinshelwood is known for his versatility but of late he has impressed in the No 10 role. He added: “I'll play anywhere the manager needs or wants me to play, but I'm really enjoying the higher position. I think I can contribute with goals and assists.

“When I first came through, I was playing full-back all the time, and I thought that was going to be me for the rest of my career.

“Last season, I had a good run in the ten role, and the manager obviously trusts me and likes me to play there.”
